intro: Verdi’s Prelude to Act I of La traviata comes before Violetta’s party and sets her high violin music beside the theme of her love song. Toscanini conducts the New York Philharmonic.

sections.label: Intro · High divided violins
sections.mNote: High violin chords sound with no bass beneath them.

sections.label: A · Violetta’s love melody in E major
sections.mNote: Strings play the melody in E major over regularly spaced bass notes.

sections.label: A′ · Cellos beneath violin figuration
sections.mNote: Cellos and bassoon carry the tune beneath quick violin decoration

sections.label: Coda · Short phrases, final E-major chord
sections.mNote: Short phrases grow fewer and close on an E-major chord.

cues.title: Opening, divided violins
cues.text: The prelude begins with the violins alone, divided into small groups and marked ppp. They play high, with no bass beneath them. Violas and a solo cello enter later.
cues.evidence: Verdi, La traviata, Ricordi full score, 1914, plate 113958, p. 1: eight solo players in each violin section, divided; viola and solo cello enter later. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/6/6c/IMSLP514870-PMLP16223-Verdi_-_La_traviata.pdf.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Letter to Emanuele Muzio, 1853
cues.text: On 7 March 1853 Verdi wrote to Emanuele Muzio about the première in Venice the night before: “La traviata last night a failure. Was the fault mine or the singers’? Time will tell.”
cues.evidence: Verdi to Emanuele Muzio, 7 March 1853, English translation quoted in the performance history at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_traviata. La Fenice première, 6 March, also documented by English National Opera: https://www.eno.org/discover-opera/articles/an-introduction-to-la-traviata/.

cues.title: Love theme, strings
cues.text: The strings play the broad E-major melody that Violetta later gives to Alfredo, “Amami, Alfredo” — “Love me, Alfredo.” She sings it in Act II before leaving him. In the Prelude the tune has no words, and the orchestra accompanies it with repeated chords.
cues.evidence: Ricordi full score, Prelude, p. 2, love theme; Piave’s libretto, Act II, Violetta’s Amami, Alfredo before her departure. The dramatic context and prelude themes are described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_traviata. Translation ours.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Melody in cellos and bassoon
cues.text: The cellos and bassoon play the long melody while the first violins decorate it with quick, detached notes. The clarinet adds a second melodic line.
cues.evidence: Ricordi full score, pp. 3–5: cello and first bassoon melody, clarinet line, divided first-violin semiquavers, repeated inner-string chords.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Dumas fils’s play, Paris, 1852
cues.text: In February 1852, in Paris with Giuseppina Strepponi, Verdi saw Dumas fils’s La Dame aux camélias. Eleven months later he told Cesare De Sanctis that his Venice subject was “of the age”, one another composer might shun for its costumes, period and “a thousand other clumsy scruples”.
cues.evidence: Oreste Bossini, “Violetta, o la moderna Maddalena”, Teatro Lirico di Cagliari programme essay: Verdi’s letter of 21 January 1852 from Paris, the play’s performance there in February 1852, and his letter to Cesare De Sanctis of 1 January 1853, “Un soggetto dell’epoca. Un altro forse non l’avrebbe fatto per i costumi, pei tempi e per altri mille goffi scrupoli” (translation ours): https://www.liricocagliari.it/archivio/media/12/85725238805832/2020_violetta_maddalena.pdf . René Weis, Royal Opera House: the play’s première at the Vaudeville on 2 February 1852, where Verdi and Strepponi probably first met the story: https://www.rbo.org.uk/news/the-real-traviata-the-tragic-true-story-that-inspired-la-traviata

cues.title: Close of the prelude in E major
cues.text: The phrases shorten. Verdi marks allargando, then diminuendo and morendo — dying away. The first violins continue their repeated notes nearly to the end, and the bass moves from B to E for a soft close in E major before the curtain rises on Violetta’s party.
cues.evidence: Ricordi full score, p. 6, final systems: allargando, diminuendo, morendo and E-major cadence. The following stage scene begins with Violetta’s party.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Bass and wind under the love melody
transitions.to: A · Violetta’s love melody in E major
transitions.how: The high violin phrase descends. Regular bass notes and short wind chords set out E major, and the first violins, violas and cellos play the love melody together, marked con espressione.
transitions.evidence: Ricordi full score, pp. 1–2: descending end of the introduction, new bass and wind accompaniment, con espressione string melody in E major.

transitions.title: The melody passes below the violins
transitions.from: A · Violetta’s love melody in E major
transitions.how: A short cello line links the two statements. The cellos then play the E-major melody with the first bassoon, and above them the divided first violins play detached semiquavers. Second violins and violas repeat their chords, and the bass keeps its spaced notes.
transitions.evidence: Ricordi full score, p. 3, cello link and decorated restatement, continuing on pp. 4–5.

transitions.title: The violin figures stop
transitions.to: Coda · Short phrases, final E-major chord
transitions.how: The melody contracts into short figures exchanged with the wind. At the allargando the bass reaches B, which prepares the final E-major chord. Verdi then marks diminuendo and morendo. The violin semiquavers continue through the softening chords and stop at the last sustained E.
transitions.evidence: Ricordi full score, p. 6, final cadential systems and printed expressive markings.

source.title: Verdi, La traviata, full score (Milan: G. Ricordi, 1914, plate 113958; Dover reprint)
source.locator: No. 1, Preludio, printed pp. 1–6; bars placed between the file’s section times

timeline.note: Eight solo violins, divided, in the highest register; nothing else sounds.
Violas and cellos enter; a solo clarinet and horn join the violins.
Cantabile in E major: the violins play over soft repeated wind notes and a plucked bass.
The tune moves to violas and cellos, supported by clarinet and bassoon, while the violins decorate it.
A solo horn enters; the clarinet plays above the divided violins.
The decoration increases, with trills and figures in the violins and short wind phrases over the cellos.
Quiet close: allargando, diminuendo, morendo, with the whole ensemble dying away.

composer.born: 10 October 1813, Le Roncole, near Busseto (then in the French Empire)
composer.epithet: Composer whose catchy tenor tunes could carry a fatal meaning when the wrong man heard them.
facts: Provesi in Busseto; private lessons with Lavigna after Milan’s Conservatoire rejected him
Milan · Venice · Florence · Rome · Naples · Paris · St Petersburg · Cairo
Piave, Cammarano and Boito were his principal collaborators
Operas from Oberto (1839) to Falstaff (1893); the Requiem, sacred music, songs and a string quartet
composer.background:
Milan’s Conservatoire turned Giuseppe Verdi down in 1832. Antonio Barezzi, a merchant from Busseto who had helped pay for his move to Milan, kept supporting him, and Verdi studied privately with Vincenzo Lavigna, formerly a musician at La Scala. He learnt counterpoint and went to the theatre. Four years later he married Barezzi’s daughter Margherita and took a municipal musical post in Busseto. His patrons had known him since he was a boy and had heard him play, and they supported him with their own money.

His parents kept an inn and shop at Le Roncole, where he was born in 1813. He learnt the organ locally, then studied with Ferdinando Provesi in nearby Busseto. Oberto, his first opera, reached La Scala in 1839 and earned him further commissions. His daughter Virginia had died in 1838; his son Icilio died in 1839, and his wife Margherita in June 1840, when Verdi was twenty-six. That September the theatre presented his comedy Un giorno di regno, which failed.
